browser-as-attack-surface.overview: The browser is where your application meets untrusted input. It also holds the most valuable things a user has: sessions, credentials, and the ability to reach authenticated systems.
how_it_works: The browser renders whatever the server sends, and it has to guess whether that content is data or instructions.
It executes scripts from many origins on the same page, so the origin is the unit of trust.
It stores state in cookies and storage, and that state becomes a target for anyone who can influence the page.
It follows redirects and loads third-party scripts, so a single compromised dependency reaches every user.
The same-origin policy is the main boundary, and most serious web flaws are ways of getting around it.
history: Static pages had no attack surface beyond the server, and the browser was mostly a renderer.
The rise of scripted pages brought cross-site scripting, which remains the most reliable way to act as a logged-in user.
Third-party advertising and analytics scripts became normal, which expanded the trusted computing base of most sites.
Browser sandboxing, site isolation and stronger privacy controls have been added in response to real abuse.
real_world: One compromised third-party script reaches every user of a site, which is a worse distribution channel than any phishing campaign.
A cross-site scripting flaw lets an attacker make authenticated requests as the victim without knowing their password.
A cookie without the right flags is readable by any script on the page, so one XSS flaw becomes full session theft.
what_to_look_for: Check what third-party scripts are loaded, and whether each one is worth the trust it is given.
Check how the response tells the browser to treat the content, rather than relying on the browser to guess.
Check which cookies are readable by scripts and which are sent automatically on every request.
Check whether authentication state is kept somewhere an injected script cannot reach.
defensive: Send explicit headers that restrict what the page may load and do, rather than relying on defaults.
Keep authentication state in cookies that scripts cannot read, with strict scope and lifetime.
Minimise and vet third-party scripts, and prefer ones you can self-host if you genuinely need them.
Use a Content Security Policy in report-only mode first, then enforce it once it is realistic.
Treat any untrusted data reaching a page as a potential XSS payload until output encoding says otherwise.

sql-command-and-template-injection.overview: Injection is what happens when data is treated as code. It is still one of the most damaging classes of web flaw because it turns data access into code execution, and it is usually a direct consequence of building queries with string concatenation.
how_it_works: A query is code; a value inside it is data. Concatenating a value into the query moves it from data into code.
SQL injection lets an attacker change the meaning of a query, which can mean reading data they should not, changing data they should not, or in some configurations running commands on the server.
Command injection is the same idea against a shell: an argument containing shell metacharacters becomes a command.
Template and expression injection is the same idea again, applied to whatever a templating engine evaluates.
The fix in every case is the same in principle: keep data in a place the interpreter will never treat as instructions.
history: Early web applications built queries by pasting request values into SQL strings, because there was no easier way.
Parameterised queries, called prepared statements, were available early but were not the default in most languages or drivers.
Object-relational mappers made query building convenient and accidentally reintroduced raw-string escaping as a fallback.
Cloud infrastructure as a service removed the easy shell escape, and pushed attackers toward reading data instead.
real_world: A login form built by concatenating the username into a query can be bypassed without knowing any password.
A report feature that shells out to render a file can be turned into arbitrary command execution.
A templating engine evaluating user-supplied expressions turns a template preview into remote code execution.
what_to_look_for: Check whether queries use parameter binding, or whether values are escaped into a string before the query runs.
Check whether a value can influence a table name, column name or sort order, since parameters cannot bind those.
Check for any call that passes user input to a shell, an evaluator or a template engine.
Check whether an ORM raw-query escape hatch is used anywhere near request data.
defensive: Use parameterised queries or prepared statements for every value, and never build SQL by concatenation.
Map any dynamic identifier from a fixed allow-list rather than accepting it from the request.
Avoid invoking a shell; use library calls that take an argument array instead of a command string.
Keep templating engines out of paths where users can supply the template or the expression.
Run the database account with the least privilege it needs, so an injection cannot read or change more than it should.

cross-site-scripting-and-output-encoding.overview: Cross-site scripting is when attacker-controlled content is treated as script by the browser. It is ranked highly because the script runs with the logged-in user's authority, so the attacker never needs a password.
how_it_works: The flaw is a missing decision about what kind of content a value is at the point it is written into the page.
Encoded correctly, a value is text. Encoded wrongly or not at all, the same value can be markup or script.
Reflected scripting delivers the payload in the request, stored scripting saves it on the server, and DOM scripting finds it in client-side code.
Stored scripting is the most damaging because it reaches every visitor and needs no lure.
A cookie scoped to the site is a strong payload: a script that steals it gets the victim's authenticated session.
history: Cross-site scripting was one of the earliest named web vulnerabilities and has been a standard top finding ever since.
Modern templating engines introduced auto-escaping, which removed most reflected flaws for teams that used them consistently.
Single-page applications moved rendering into the browser, so flaws moved from the server into client-side code.
Content Security Policy and cookie flags were added as a second layer because encoding alone cannot catch every context.
real_world: A search page that echoes the query without encoding lets an attacker send a link that steals a session when clicked.
A comment stored and later rendered on every page turns one user's post into a compromise of every reader.
Client-side code that writes a value into the page with innerHTML reintroduces the flaw despite a safe backend.
what_to_look_for: Check whether output is encoded for the specific context it lands in: HTML body, attribute, URL, JavaScript or CSS are different.
Check client-side code for direct writes of untrusted values into the page.
Check whether the session cookie is readable by scripts, which decides how bad a single flaw becomes.
Check whether a content security policy exists and is actually enforced rather than only reported.
defensive: Encode output for its context, and prefer frameworks that do this by default and only switch off when you must.
Keep session cookies HttpOnly so a script cannot read them even if one gets through.
Deploy a content security policy without unsafe-inline, so injected script is not allowed to run.
Use templating rather than building markup by concatenation, and sanitise where HTML is genuinely required.
Treat content security policy violations as reports to fix, not noise to ignore.

broken-access-control-and-idor.overview: Broken access control is the top category in the current OWASP list, and the reason is structural: applications grant access in many places, and any one of them being wrong is a breach. Insecure direct object reference is its most common form.
how_it_works: An access decision needs the identity, the action and the specific object, and a check that omits the object is not a check.
A sequential identifier in a URL is an invitation: if /invoice/41 fails, /invoice/42 probably works.
Correct checks are often present on the list page and missing on the detail, edit or delete endpoint.
Client-side hiding of a control is not enforcement, because the request can be sent directly.
Bulk endpoints are especially risky, because one request can act on many objects at once.
history: Early applications assumed a user either saw everything or nothing, so per-object checks were rarely written.
The transition to many customers on one system made per-object checks necessary, and the gap was never fully closed.
The industry survey has ranked broken access control near the top for several editions, and it is first in the 2025 list.
Centralised policy and relationship-based access control are the current direction for avoiding scattered decisions.
real_world: Changing an identifier in a URL returns another customer's data, which is one of the most common serious findings in testing.
A delete endpoint with no ownership check lets a user remove records that are not theirs.
An administrative action guarded only by a hidden menu item is reachable by anyone who knows the URL.
what_to_look_for: Check every endpoint that takes an object identifier and ask whether it verifies permission for that object.
Check whether identifiers are guessable, and whether guessing is rate-limited or detected.
Check whether administrative functionality is separated from ordinary functionality, not just styled differently.
Check whether any endpoint accepts an identifier list, since per-object checks are often skipped for bulk actions.
defensive: Default to deny and grant explicitly, so an unimplemented check fails closed rather than open.
Enforce the check on the server for every request, and make it part of the data access layer rather than the route.
Use unguessable identifiers as defence in depth, not as a replacement for a check.
Rate-limit and log authorisation failures, since a burst of them is a clear signal.
Test every endpoint with two accounts of different privilege; this finds these flaws faster than any scanner.

security-misconfiguration-default-creden.overview: Misconfiguration is the second category in the current list, and it is the one most likely to be found by anyone, because it involves no clever technique at all. Default credentials are the extreme case of it.
how_it_works: Every platform ships with defaults, and many defaults are designed to get you running quickly rather than secure.
A service that is only supposed to be reachable internally is often reachable from anywhere because the rule allowing it is too broad.
Verbose errors, directory listings and default paths disclose exactly the information an attacker needs for the next step.
Unnecessary features, sample applications and unused accounts are left in place because removing them was never required.
Configuration drift means the documented secure baseline and the running system quietly stop matching.
history: Manual server configuration meant every machine was slightly different, so nobody could claim to know the state.
Configuration management tools made baselines repeatable and comparison possible.
Cloud platforms moved much configuration to a console, which made it visible but also easy to leave permissive.
Modern platforms increasingly ship secure by default, which raises the value of checking what was changed.
real_world: A database or storage service reachable from the internet with a default account is found within minutes of appearing.
Verbose stack traces disclose framework versions, which narrows the search for applicable weaknesses from years to hours.
A backup or administrative interface left enabled months after a migration is a common finding.
what_to_look_for: Check every service that should not be public, and verify it from outside rather than from inside.
Check for default accounts, sample content and documentation endpoints.
Check error verbosity, since a detailed error is a free reconnaissance tool.
Compare the running configuration against the documented baseline, and fail when they differ.
defensive: Automate a hardened baseline and verify it continuously, because manual checks stop being done.
Remove default accounts, sample applications and unused features as part of installation, not later.
Return generic errors to users and keep the detail in a log the user cannot read.
Restrict administrative and management interfaces to specific addresses and strong authentication.
Fail compliance checks loudly, so drift is caught by the pipeline rather than by an auditor.

vulnerable-and-outdated-components.overview: The 2021 list called this vulnerable and outdated components. The 2025 list broadened it into software supply chain failures, because the risk is rarely only in a library you chose yourself.
how_it_works: A dependency you did not write is code you are responsible for, and it is usually a large share of what you ship.
A component advisory matters only in context: if the vulnerable function is never called, the practical risk is different.
Transitive dependencies mean a vulnerability can arrive through something you never named.
A compromised package version is a supply chain attack, and version pinning is what makes it possible.
An unmaintained component will never receive a fix, so exposure grows without anyone choosing it.
history: Component reuse accelerated development and quietly transferred a large amount of security responsibility to third parties.
Software composition analysis tooling made dependency inventories practical and sharply increased the visible number of findings.
Compromised maintainer accounts and malicious package versions turned a maintenance question into a security one.
The 2025 list responded by renaming and widening the category to cover the whole chain rather than the library alone.
real_world: A widely used library maintainer's account is taken over, and every application pulling that version is exposed within hours.
An application inherits hundreds of transitive dependencies, and only a generated inventory shows what is actually there.
A component used for a single convenience function can be the largest single risk in the build.
what_to_look_for: Check whether a machine-readable inventory of dependencies exists and includes transitive components.
Check whether advisories are monitored and acted on, and against what prioritisation.
Check build pipelines for unpinned versions and for install scripts that execute third-party code.
Check whether any component is unmaintained, since those will never be fixed.
defensive: Generate a dependency inventory in the build and fail the build on new high-severity findings.
Pin versions and use lock files, so a build is reproducible and cannot silently pull a new version.
Prioritise by reachability: whether the vulnerable code path is actually used in your product.
Remove unused dependencies, since a component nobody uses is risk with no benefit.
Restrict what build steps and install scripts can do, and monitor upstream sources for new advisories.

file-uploads-ssrf-and-input-validation.overview: Input validation, file handling and server-side requests are grouped together because they share one root cause: the application lets untrusted input decide what the server does next.
how_it_works: Validation has to happen on the server, on the parsed value, not only in the browser form.
A file upload is dangerous because the filename, the declared type and the actual content can all differ.
If uploaded files are served from the same origin as the application, a crafted file can run as script against your own users.
Server-side request forgery happens when a URL from a user decides where the server connects, which reaches things the user cannot.
Server-side request forgery is especially useful against cloud metadata services, which return credentials to whoever asks.
history: Client-side validation was long treated as validation, and it protected nothing once the request was sent directly.
Web shells arrived through file uploads, and the fix was separating storage from execution.
Server-side request forgery was named once cloud metadata services made it valuable, and it remains a default-credential route.
Modern frameworks do more validation by default, which helps only where teams use the built-in mechanism.
real_world: An upload directory inside the web root means a crafted HTML or SVG file executes in the site's origin.
A preview feature that fetches a user-supplied URL can be aimed at an internal metadata endpoint and return credentials.
A file-type check based on the extension or the client-declared content type is defeated trivially.
what_to_look_for: Check where uploaded files are stored and whether they are served with a content type that cannot execute.
Check whether validation happens server-side, on the value after parsing.
Check every feature that takes a URL and fetches it, and see whether the destination is restricted.
Check whether the fetch follows redirects, since a redirect can bypass an allow-list.
defensive: Store uploads outside the web root, and serve them with a neutral content type and a content disposition of attachment.
Validate on the server against the actual content, not the filename or the declared type.
Rewrite or re-enable nothing at runtime: if the server must render a file, sanitise it rather than trusting it.
For server-side requests, allow-list destinations, resolve the address, and re-check after every redirect.
Block access to instance metadata endpoints from application workloads at the network layer.

web-defences-csp-hsts-samesite-and-csrf-.overview: These are the browser-side defences that limit what happens when something else goes wrong. None of them prevents a vulnerability; each of them reduces how much an attacker gets from one.
how_it_works: A content security policy tells the browser which sources of script, style and frames are allowed, so injected script may simply not run.
HTTP strict transport security tells the browser to refuse plaintext, which removes a network-level downgrade.
SameSite on cookies decides whether they are attached to cross-site requests, which is the mechanism behind most cross-site request forgery.
A cross-site request forgery token is a value the attacker cannot read, so a forged request cannot include it.
These controls work together: one blocks the script, one blocks the request, and the other forces the browser to a safe protocol.
history: These headers were added to browsers one at a time, and adoption lagged for years because they broke real applications.
Report-only modes were introduced so sites could measure impact before enforcing, which is the only realistic adoption path.
Modern frameworks enable them by default, which has moved them from an expert concern to a baseline expectation.
Third-party script requirements are the main reason policies stay permissive, which is the same trust problem as before.
real_world: A site with no content security policy turns one stored scripting flaw into a complete account takeover.
A session cookie with no SameSite attribute is sent on cross-site requests, which is exactly what makes forgery work.
HSTS missing from a site allows a network attacker to downgrade the first request, which is often the only one that matters.
what_to_look_for: Check the response headers directly, because configuration that works locally may not reach production.
Check whether the session cookie has Secure, HttpOnly and an appropriate SameSite value.
Check whether a content security policy is enforced or only reported.
Check whether any state-changing action relies solely on a cookie with no token.
defensive: Send a content security policy in report-only mode, fix what it flags, then enforce without unsafe-inline.
Set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on every session cookie, and use the strictest SameSite your flows allow.
Enable HTTP strict transport security, including preloading once you are confident it will not break anything.
Require a token on every state-changing request, and treat the token check as the authorisation check too.
Test with the headers enabled in a real browser, since some failures only appear with a real session.

owasp-top-10-2025-reading-the-list.overview: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document, not a standard. Read it as a map of where real breaches come from, not as a checklist that proves an application is safe.
how_it_works: It is built from data contributed about real applications, so the ranking reflects frequency and impact rather than technical novelty.

The 2025 list is broken access control, security misconfiguration, software supply chain failures, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, authentication failures, software or data integrity failures, security logging and alerting failures, and mishandling of exceptional conditions.
Broken access control is first because it has the widest set of underlying weaknesses, not because it is the most interesting.
Each category points to dozens of specific weaknesses, so the list is an index rather than a description.
A category you are not exposed to is not a category you can ignore entirely, because the same mistake appears under several headings.
history: The first Top 10 was produced from a contributor survey and became the de facto awareness document for web security within a few years.
The 2021 edition reorganised categories and dropped several that were better solved than they once were.
The 2025 edition widened the supply chain category and added a focus on mishandling of exceptional conditions, reflecting observed failure patterns.
It has always been a starting point, and the project says so: the list is awareness, the cheat sheets are practice.
real_world: An organisation that treats a clean Top 10 scan as a security programme has confused a checklist for a process.
The most common findings still cluster in the first two categories, which is why they stay at the top.
The categories cover the web application, so the largest risks in many organisations are entirely outside this list.
what_to_look_for: Use the list to decide what to test and what to build habits around, not to produce a pass or fail result.
For each category, ask whether it applies to what you actually run, and record the reasoning.
Follow the linked cheat sheets, since the list deliberately does not contain the fix.
Treat a finding in a category you were not expecting as a signal that your process has a gap.
defensive: Work the categories in order, because the first two catch more real risk than the rest combined.
Use the cheat sheets and the application security verification standard as your implementation reference.
Add automated checks for the mechanically detectable categories and use manual testing for access control and design.
Feed findings back into code review and pipeline checks so the same category is not rediscovered every quarter.
Keep the list as awareness for a wider audience, and use a more rigorous standard for the work itself.
